comment: Every entry of the server's declared `mcp.limits` must appear here exactly once, and selftest.js fails if the two key sets differ. A limit an agent plans against has to have pinned, observable behaviour at its boundary; one that is declared and never exercised is a claim, not a control.

coverageKinds.boundary: A pair of real sources: one just under the declared value that succeeds, one just over it that fails in the stated way. Run against the live server on every selftest.
coverageKinds.hostGate: Enforced by the adapter before or around execution, so it is exercised through the server's own admission path rather than through a source program.
coverageKinds.injectedLimit: Not reachable at the declared value within `wallTimeMs`, so the boundary is pinned in Rust with a small injected ceiling instead. The `rustTest` field names that test.

sourceBytes.note: Rejected by the adapter on UTF-8 byte length before a backend is entered. The engine applies the same 65536-byte ceiling as `ResourceLimitExceeded { resource: sourceBytes }` if a host ever forwards a larger program.

over.source: 2 SQRT 3 SQRT + 5 SQRT 7 SQRT + * 11 SQRT 13 SQRT + * 17 SQRT 19 SQRT + *

wallTimeMs.note: The over case is a product of four two-radical sums. Its cost grows roughly twelvefold per additional factor, so it is many times over the ceiling rather than marginally over it; the under case completes in well under a second.

responseBytes.note: Both backends measure the same thing: UTF-8 bytes of the schema-1 envelope text. `backend/parity-test.js` runs this pair against both, which is what the native-only `maxBuffer` implementation could never have shown.

concurrentExecutions.note: Exercised through `ExecutionGate` in selftest.js: the gate admits exactly its capacity, queues a further caller for up to CAPACITY_WAIT_MS, hands a released slot to the longest-waiting caller, and answers `capacityExhausted` with `retryable: true` only when the wait elapses.

materializedElements.note: A generative ceiling is a reason-carrying NIL, not an error: the program is well formed and the absence is recoverable with `^`.

numericWork.note: Charged on every rational and algebraic operation in every operand shape, priced as lanes x limb-multiply units. Two earlier reasons for injectedLimit are gone: arithmetic outside the scalar-shaped path is charged now, and a refusal no longer loses its diagnosis to responseBytes (an error report elides the stack values it cannot afford -- see agent::error_stack, and the `a huge failing stack does not cost the diagnosis` golden case). What remains is a timing relationship. A source reaching 10,000,000 units does exist inside sourceBytes -- `[ 0 99999 ] RANGE` plus 101 additions charges 10,100,000 and is refused by name in about 7 KB -- but it spends 5.2s on the reference container's debug build, past the 5000ms wallTimeMs, so wallTimeMs would decide the case and not this ceiling. The two prices disagree because the meter charges one unit per one-limb lane while a boxed per-element operation costs far more wall time than a limb multiply: that lane path runs at roughly 7,700 units/ms against the 57,000-86,000 the scalar chains were calibrated at. Going the other way -- widening operands instead of multiplying lanes -- bigintBits always fires first, because reaching 10,000,000 units by repeated multiplication needs an operand wider than 4,096 limbs by construction. Ordering the three ceilings so each is independently reachable inside wallTimeMs is the open calibration question; it is not a gap in what is charged.

bigintBits.note: Bounds the width of any exact arithmetic result, rational as well as algebraic, in every operand shape. Plain rational arithmetic used to pass through no size guard at all: 400 chained multiplications of a 4096-digit literal, 0.4% of the executionSteps budget, spent 40 seconds building a multi-megabyte integer with every ceiling silent. Then the scalar-shaped path was charged and the shape axis was left open -- only push_scalar_fastpath_result and push_exact_real_schema_result charged, both requiring both operands to be scalar-shaped, so [ 1 21000 ] RANGE [ 1 ] { * } FOLD returned a 271,233-bit integer metered at zero while the same fold with a scalar accumulator was refused. Charging and size-checking now sit at the dispatch entry (interpreter/arithmetic_meter.rs), priced as lanes x operand width, so a scalar is the one-lane case of the same formula and both folds are refused at the same 10,000,573 units. Still injectedLimit rather than boundary for the ordering reason given under numericWork: repeated multiplication by a 4096-digit literal crosses 262,144 bits at about the same point it crosses 10,000,000 work units, so a boundary pair here would be pinned five percent away from a different ceiling and would break confusingly when either price is re-measured.

algebraicTerms.note: Reaching 4096 terms needs twelve doublings of a two-radical sum. With work priced by width the cascade is charged about 16,000,000 units before the twelfth doubling lands, so numericWork at its declared 10,000,000 now fires first: this ceiling remains unreachable, for a different reason than before. Ordering the two so each is independently observable is part of the same follow-up as the block-arithmetic gap.
